processing: Details are not documented. Wuyi rock teas in general are shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted.
harvest_season: Not documented; Wuyi rock teas are normally picked in spring.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: dark, twisted strips.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting record exists. What can be expected is only what is typical of Wuyi rock teas: roast, mineral depth and floral sweetness.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas: water near the boil and short steeps.

vintage_note: How this one is sold is not documented. Wuyi rock teas are usually labelled by spring harvest year and roast, and a tea this obscure would be a small lot at most.
description:
Yu Jing Liu Xiang is a Wuyi famous-bush name that is very poorly documented. The characters read as jade well and flowing fragrance, and that is about as far as firm ground goes.

What can be said about the making is what holds for the class: Wuyi rock teas are shaken, partly oxidised and roasted.

Treat any tasting promise with caution. Expect the broad pattern of the class and brew it the same way, hot and short.

If you meet this name on sale, ask the seller what bush it comes from and where it grew.
history: Little is documented. No reliable record of its origin, its first mention or the person who made it known is available.
